sentences.zh: 歷武陵、始興太守，遷大司農，卒於官。

translations.literal: He served as grand administrator of Wuling and Shixing, rose to Minister of Agriculture, and died in office.
translations.idiomatic: He governed Wuling and Shixing, became minister of agriculture, and died in harness.

sentences.zh: 卞壼字望之，濟陰冤句人也。

translations.literal: Bian Kun, courtesy name Wangzhi, was a native of Yuanju in Jiyin.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun, style Wangzhi, was a man of Yuanju in Jiyin.

sentences.zh: 祖統，琅邪內史。

translations.literal: His grandfather Tong was interior minister of Langya.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Bian Tong had been interior minister of Langya.

sentences.zh: 父粹，以清辯鑒察稱。

translations.literal: His father Cui was famed for clear disputation and keen judgment.
translations.idiomatic: His father Bian Cui was celebrated for lucid argument and sharp discernment.

sentences.zh: 兄弟六人並登宰府，世稱「卞氏六龍，玄仁無雙」。

translations.literal: Six brothers together ascended to ministerial offices; the age called them “the six dragons of the Bian clan—none matched Xuaren.”
translations.idiomatic: Six brothers reached high ministry together; contemporaries called them the six dragons of the Bian house, with none the equal of Xuaren.

sentences.zh: 玄仁，粹字也。

translations.literal: Xuaren was Cui’s courtesy name.
translations.idiomatic: “Xuaren” was Bian Cui’s courtesy name.

sentences.zh: 弟裒，嘗忤其郡將。

translations.literal: His younger brother Pou once offended his commandery general.
translations.idiomatic: His brother Bian Pou once crossed the regional commander.

sentences.zh: 郡將怒訐其門內之私，粹遂以不訓見譏議，陵遲積年。

translations.literal: The commandery general angrily denounced private matters within Pou’s household, and Cui therefore came under censure as failing to instruct his family; for years he was held back.
translations.idiomatic: The commander retaliated with gossip about the Bian household, so Cui was faulted for lax family discipline and languished for years.

sentences.zh: 惠帝初，爲尚書郎。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Emperor Hui’s reign he became a gentleman of the Palace Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Hui took the throne he entered the palace secretariat as a gentleman.

sentences.zh: 楊駿執政，人多附會，而粹正直不阿。

translations.literal: When Yang Jun held power, many men attached themselves to him, but Cui was upright and did not curry favor.
translations.idiomatic: While Yang Jun dominated the court, flatterers swarmed him; Bian Cui stayed straight and aloof.

sentences.zh: 及駿誅，超拜右丞，封成陽子，稍遷至右軍將軍。

translations.literal: When Jun was executed, Cui was abruptly promoted to right aide and enfeoffed as village marquis of Chengyang, and by stages rose to General of the Right Army.
translations.idiomatic: After Yang Jun fell, Cui vaulted to right secretariat aide, village marquis of Chengyang, and eventually General of the Right Army.

sentences.zh: 張華之誅，粹以華婿免官。

translations.literal: At Zhang Hua’s execution, Cui was dismissed from office as Zhang Hua’s son-in-law.
translations.idiomatic: When Zhang Hua died, Cui lost his post as Zhang’s son-in-law.

sentences.zh: 齊王冏輔政，爲侍中、中書令，進爵爲公。

translations.literal: When Prince Sima Jiong of Qi assisted the government, Cui became palace attendant and palace secretary and was advanced in fief to duke.
translations.idiomatic: Under Prince Sima Jiong of Qi he served as palace attendant and palace secretary and was raised to a ducal fief.

sentences.zh: 及長沙王乂專權，粹立朝正色，乂忌而害之。

translations.literal: When Prince Sima Yi of Changsha monopolized power, Cui stood in court with stern dignity; Yi resented him and killed him.
translations.idiomatic: When Prince Sima Yi of Changsha seized power, Cui faced court with icy dignity; Yi envied him and had him killed.

sentences.zh: 初，粹如廁，見物若兩眼，俄而難作。

translations.literal: Earlier, when Cui went to the privy, he saw something like two eyes; shortly afterward the disaster occurred.
translations.idiomatic: Once, relieving himself, Cui saw what looked like two eyes in the dark; soon after came his death.

sentences.zh: 壼弱冠有名譽司、兗二州。

translations.literal: Kun at the capping age had reputation in the two provinces of Si and Yan.
translations.idiomatic: By his capping year Kun’s name was known across Si and Yan provinces.

sentences.zh: 齊王冏辟皆不就。

translations.literal: When Prince Sima Jiong of Qi summoned him, he did not go on any of the occasions.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Sima Jiong repeatedly summoned him; he never took office.

sentences.zh: 遇家禍，還鄉里。

translations.literal: He encountered his family’s disaster and returned to his home village.
translations.idiomatic: After the slaughter of his kin he withdrew to his home district.

sentences.zh: 永嘉中，除著作郎，襲父爵。

translations.literal: In the Yongjia years he was appointed gentleman editor and inherited his father’s noble rank.
translations.idiomatic: During Yongjia he became gentleman editor and succeeded to his father’s title.

sentences.zh: 征東將軍周馥請爲從事中郎，不就。

translations.literal: General Who Conquers the East, Zhou Fu, asked him to serve as attendant clerk, but he did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Fu, east-conquering general, wanted him as attendant clerk; he refused.

sentences.zh: 遭本州傾覆，東依妻兄徐州刺史裴盾。

translations.literal: When his native province collapsed, he went east to rely on his wife’s elder brother, Pei Dun, Inspector of Xu Province.
translations.idiomatic: When Jiyin fell he fled east to his brother-in-law Pei Dun, inspector of Xu province.

sentences.zh: 盾以壼行廣陵相。

translations.literal: Dun had Kun act as acting grand administrator of Guangling.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Dun made him acting grand administrator of Guangling.

sentences.zh: 元帝鎮建鄴，召爲從事中郎，委以選舉，甚見親杖。

translations.literal: When Emperor Yuan was stationed at Jianye, he summoned Kun as attendant clerk, entrusted him with selections for office, and treated him with great intimacy and reliance.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan at Jianye named him attendant clerk, handed him appointments, and leaned on him heavily.

sentences.zh: 出爲明帝東中郎長史。

translations.literal: He went out as senior clerk to the heir apparent’s east-center general, Emperor Ming.
translations.idiomatic: He later became senior clerk to the heir apparent’s eastern-center army—the future Emperor Ming.

sentences.zh: 遭繼母憂，既葬，起復舊職，累辭不就。

translations.literal: He suffered mourning for a stepmother; after the burial, he was recalled to his old posts, but he repeatedly declined and would not go.
translations.idiomatic: When his stepmother died he buried her, then was recalled to his old posts but declined again and again.

sentences.zh: 元帝遣中使敦逼，壼牋自陳曰：

translations.literal: Emperor Yuan sent inner envoys to press him urgently; Kun submitted a note stating himself, saying,
translations.idiomatic: The emperor sent eunuchs to insist; Kun answered with a personal note:

sentences.zh: 壼天性狷狹，不能和俗，退以情事，欲畢志家門。

translations.literal: “Kun by nature is narrow and unyielding and cannot harmonize with the vulgar world; retiring on personal grounds, he wished to fulfill his resolve within his household.
translations.idiomatic: “I am stiff-necked and cannot swim with the crowd; I meant to retire and live out my days at home.

sentences.zh: 亡父往爲中書令，時壼蒙大例，望門見辟，信其所執，得不祗就。

translations.literal: My late father once was palace secretary; at that time Kun fell under the great precedent of seeing the gate summoned and, trusting what he held to, was able not to accept respectfully.
translations.idiomatic: When my late father was palace secretary I was swept up in the usual summons to serve; I trusted my principles and refused the honor.

sentences.zh: 門戶遇禍，迸竄易名，得存視息，私志有素。

translations.literal: The gate of our house met disaster; I fled in hiding and changed my name, barely preserving breath and sight; my private resolve has long been fixed.
translations.idiomatic: Our house was ruined; I fled under an alias and barely survived—my mind was set long ago.

sentences.zh: 加嬰極難，流寄蘭陵，爲苟晞所召，恐見逼迫，依下邳裴盾，又見假授，思暫之郡，規得託身。

translations.literal: Added to that were the utmost hardships of infancy; drifting I lodged at Lanling; summoned by Gou Xi, I feared being compelled, and relied on Pei Dun of Xiapi; again I received a provisional appointment, thinking only to reach the commandery for a time, planning to obtain a place to entrust my body.
translations.idiomatic: I was a child in chaos, drifted to Lanling, was dragooned by Gou Xi, fled to Pei Dun at Xiapi, took a temporary post only to find shelter.

sentences.zh: 尋蒙見召，爲從事中郎，豈曰貪榮，直欲自致，規暫恭命，行當乞退。

translations.literal: Soon I received a summons to be attendant clerk—was it greed for glory? I wished only to answer briefly, intending for the moment to obey the order and then beg to withdraw.
translations.idiomatic: When you called me attendant clerk it was not ambition—I meant to obey briefly, then resign.

sentences.zh: 屬華軼之難，不敢自陳。

translations.literal: It happened that the troubles of Hua Yi came; I did not dare state myself plainly.
translations.idiomatic: Then Hua Yi’s rebellion broke; I dared not speak plainly.

sentences.zh: 軼既梟懸，壼亦嬰病，具自歸聞，未蒙恕遣。

translations.literal: Once Yi was beheaded with his head displayed, Kun also fell ill; I fully reported myself and begged leave, yet was not granted merciful dismissal.
translations.idiomatic: After Hua Yi’s head hung on the wall I fell ill, reported in full, and still was refused compassionate leave.

sentences.zh: 世子北征，選寵顯望，復以無施，忝充元佐。

translations.literal: When the heir apparent marched north, choosing men of honored repute, again, though I had nothing to offer, I was disgraced by filling the post of chief aide.
translations.idiomatic: When the heir apparent campaigned north he picked men of rank; though I had no merit I was shamed by serving as chief aide.

sentences.zh: 榮則榮矣，實非素懷。

translations.literal: The glory was glory, yet it was not my original intent.
translations.idiomatic: The honor glittered, but it was never what I wanted.

sentences.zh: 顧以命重人輕，不敢辭憚。

translations.literal: Only because the charge was weighty and the man slight, I did not dare decline from fear.
translations.idiomatic: The duty was grave and I too small to refuse out of cowardice.

sentences.zh: 聞西臺召壼爲尚書郎，實欲因此以避賢路，未及陳誠，奄丁窮罰。

translations.literal: I heard the western desk summoned Kun as gentleman of the Palace Secretariat; I truly wished thereby to yield the path to worthies; before I could state my sincerity, suddenly I was struck by the utmost bereavement.
translations.idiomatic: I heard the western administration wanted me as palace gentleman—my chance to step aside for better men—then sudden mourning struck.

sentences.zh: 壼年九歲，爲先母弟表所見孤背。

translations.literal: When Kun was nine sui, he was orphaned and cast off, as seen by his maternal uncle Biao.
translations.idiomatic: At nine I was orphaned and abandoned by my uncle Biao on my mother’s side.

sentences.zh: 十二，蒙亡母張所見覆育。

translations.literal: At twelve sui, he received covering nurture from his late mother, Lady Zhang.
translations.idiomatic: At twelve my late mother, Lady Zhang, sheltered and raised me.

sentences.zh: 壼以陋賤，不能榮親，家產屢空，養道多闕，存無歡娛，終不備禮，拊心永恨，五內抽割。

translations.literal: Kun, mean and lowly, was unable to bring honor to his kin; the family’s property was repeatedly empty, and the way of support was much deficient; while they lived there was no joy, and in the end the full rites could not be prepared; beating his breast he harbors everlasting regret, and his five viscera are torn as if cut.
translations.idiomatic: I was too poor to honor my parents; our goods ran out, mourning rites went unfulfilled, and grief still tears my vitals.

sentences.zh: 於公無效如彼，私情艱苦如此，實無情顏昧冒榮進。

translations.literal: Thus toward the public he was as ineffective as that, while private feeling is bitter as this—truly he has no face shamelessly to risk advancing for glory.
translations.idiomatic: I have failed the state so little yet my private grief runs so deep—I cannot shamelessly chase rank.

sentences.zh: 若廢壼一人，江北便有傾危之慮，壼居事之日功績以隆者，誠不得私其身。

translations.literal: If Kun is dismissed, north of the Yangzi there will be concern of toppling peril; on the days when Kun held office his merit and deeds did indeed rise—truly he could not favor his private person.
translations.idiomatic: If you remove me the north shore may totter; while I served my work did swell—I could not favor myself.

sentences.zh: 今東中郎岐嶷自然，神明日茂，軍司馬、諸參佐並以明德宣力王事，壼之去留，曾無損益。

translations.literal: Now the heir apparent’s east-center general is naturally keen and alert, his divine intelligence daily flourishing; the army marshal and the various staff advisers all by bright virtue exert their strength on the king’s affairs—whether Kun stays or goes is of no gain or loss.
translations.idiomatic: The eastern-center heir is bright and growing wiser daily; his marshal and staff all serve with clear virtue—my presence or absence changes nothing.

sentences.zh: 賀循、謝端、顧景、丁琛、傅晞等皆荷恩命，高枕家門。

translations.literal: He Xun, Xie Duan, Gu Jing, Ding Chen, Fu Xi, and others have all received gracious commands and rest easy at their gates.
translations.idiomatic: He Xun, Xie Duan, Gu Jing, Ding Chen, Fu Xi, and the like already enjoy imperial favor at home.

sentences.zh: 壼委質二府，漸冉五載，考效則不能已彰，論心則頻累恭順，柰何哀孤之日不見愍恕哉！

translations.literal: Kun has pledged body to two administrations and has gradually passed five years; in examination of deeds he could not already make them brilliant, yet in discussion of mind he has repeatedly been respectful and compliant—how is it that on the day of mourning this orphan he does not see pity and forgiveness!”
translations.idiomatic: I have served two offices five years—little glory, much obedience—yet in my orphan’s mourning you grant no mercy!”

sentences.zh: 帝以其辭苦，不奪其志。

translations.literal: The emperor, because his words were bitter, did not wrest away his resolve.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor, moved by his bitter plea, let him keep his resolve.

sentences.zh: 服闋，爲世子師。

translations.literal: When mourning was completed, he became tutor to the heir apparent.
translations.idiomatic: After mourning ended he became tutor to the heir apparent.

sentences.zh: 壼前後居師佐之任，盡匡輔之節，一府貴而憚焉。

translations.literal: Kun, in successive posts as tutor and aide, exhausted the integrity of one who corrects and assists; the whole princely administration honored and feared him.
translations.idiomatic: As tutor and chief aide he gave full measure of candid counsel; the whole princely household stood in awe.

sentences.zh: 中興建，補太子中庶子，轉散騎常侍，侍講東宮。

translations.literal: When the Restoration was founded, he was appointed junior mentor to the heir apparent, transferred to cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, and lectured in the Eastern Palace.
translations.idiomatic: At the founding of Eastern Jin he became junior mentor to the heir apparent, then cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, lecturing in the eastern palace.

sentences.zh: 遷太子詹事，以公事免。

translations.literal: He was promoted to mentor to the heir apparent and removed for an administrative matter.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to mentor to the heir apparent, then was dismissed over a bureaucratic affair.

sentences.zh: 尋復職，轉御史中丞。

translations.literal: Soon he was restored to office and transferred to imperial censor-in-chief.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon reinstated and made imperial censor-in-chief.

sentences.zh: 忠於事上，權貴屏跡。

translations.literal: He was loyal in serving his superiors, and the powerful and noble withdrew from his path.
translations.idiomatic: He served the throne with loyalty; the mighty gave him a wide berth.

sentences.zh: 時淮南小中正王式繼母，前夫終，更適式父。

translations.literal: At that time the minor rectifier of Huainan, Wang Shi, had a stepmother who, when her former husband died, remarried Shi’s father.
translations.idiomatic: The minor Huainan rectifier Wang Shi had a stepmother who, after her first husband died, married Wang Shi’s father.

sentences.zh: 式父終，喪服訖，議還前夫家。

translations.literal: When Shi’s father died and mourning was finished, it was debated whether she should return to her former husband’s family.
translations.idiomatic: When Wang Shi’s father died and mourning ended, officials debated sending her back to her first husband’s house.

sentences.zh: 前夫家亦有繼子，奉養至終，遂合葬於前夫。

translations.literal: The former husband’s family also had a stepson who had supported her to the end, so they jointly buried her with the former husband.
translations.idiomatic: That household too had a foster son who had supported her through life, so she was buried with her first spouse.

sentences.zh: 式自云：「父臨終，母求去，父許諾。

translations.literal: Shi himself said, “When my father was dying, my mother asked to leave, and my father promised her.”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Shi claimed that on his father’s deathbed his stepmother asked to leave and his father agreed.

sentences.zh: 」於是制出母齊衰期。

translations.literal: ” Thereupon it was ruled that for a divorced mother there should be one year’s zīcuī mourning.
translations.idiomatic: The court then ruled one year of zīcuī mourning for a divorced mother.

sentences.zh: 壼奏曰：「就如式父臨終許諾，必也正名，依禮爲無所據。

translations.literal: Kun memorialized, saying, “Even supposing, as Shi claims, that his father on his deathbed gave a promise, if one must set the name aright, according to ritual there is no basis for it.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun answered: “Even if the deathbed promise were true, it has no footing in canonical ritual once names are set straight.

sentences.zh: 若夫有命，須顯七出之責，當存時棄之，無緣以絕義之妻留家制服。

translations.literal: If the husband had issued a command, one must display the responsibility of the seven grounds for divorce; she should have been cast off while he lived—there is no reason to keep in the house, in full mourning garb, a wife whose bond of duty has been severed.
translations.idiomatic: If a husband truly repudiated a wife, the “seven outs” must be explicit; she should have left while he lived—there is no warrant to lodge a severed wife at home and mourn her like a mother.

sentences.zh: 若式父臨困謬亂，使去留自由者，此必爲相要以非禮，則存亡無所得從，式宜正之以禮。

translations.literal: If, when Shi’s father lay in extremity, in delirious confusion he let her go or stay at will, that must have been a private pact contrary to ritual; then neither living nor dead can be followed, and Shi ought to have corrected it by ritual.
translations.idiomatic: If a dying man rambled and let her come and go at whim, that was an illicit private bargain; neither living nor dead can answer for it, and Wang Shi should have corrected it with ritual.

sentences.zh: 魏顆父命不從其亂，陳乾昔欲以二婢子殉，其子以非禮不從，春秋、禮記善之。

translations.literal: Wei Ke did not follow his father’s confused command; Chen Qianxi wished to bury two concubines’ sons alive with him, and his son refused as contrary to ritual—the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Record of Rites praise them.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Ke ignored a muddled paternal order; Chen Qianxi’s son refused to bury living attendants with his father—both cases are praised in the classics.

sentences.zh: 並以妾媵，猶正以禮，況其母乎！

translations.literal: Even for concubines they set ritual aright; how much more for a mother!
translations.idiomatic: They upheld ritual even for concubines—how much more for a mother!

sentences.zh: 式母於夫，生事奉終，非爲既絕之妻。

translations.literal: Shi’s mother toward her husband, while he lived, served him to the end; she was not a wife already severed.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Shi’s stepmother served her husband to the grave; she was never a “divorced” wife.

sentences.zh: 夫亡制服，不爲無義之婦。

translations.literal: When the husband died she wore mourning; she did not become a woman without duty.
translations.idiomatic: She donned widow’s weeds for him; she was no faithless woman.

sentences.zh: 自云守節，非爲更嫁。

translations.literal: She herself says she kept her chastity; she did not intend to remarry.
translations.idiomatic: She calls herself chaste, not seeking remarriage.

sentences.zh: 離絕之斷，在夫沒之後。

translations.literal: The break of severance comes after the husband’s death.
translations.idiomatic: Repudiation applies only after the husband is gone.

sentences.zh: 夫之既沒，是其從子之日，而式以爲出母，此母以子出也。

translations.literal: Once the husband is gone, that is the day she follows her son, yet Shi treats her as a divorced mother—this is a mother cast out by the son.
translations.idiomatic: After the husband died she rightly followed her son; calling her “divorced” is the son casting out his mother.

sentences.zh: 致使存無所容居，沒無所託也。

translations.literal: It causes her while alive to have nowhere to dwell, and when dead nowhere to be entrusted.
translations.idiomatic: Alive, she has no place to stand; dead, no resting place.

sentences.zh: 寄命於他人之門，埋尸於無名之冢。

translations.literal: She must entrust her life to another’s gate and bury her corpse in a nameless mound.
translations.idiomatic: She must beg another household for shelter and sleep in an unmarked grave.

sentences.zh: 若式父亡後，母尋沒於式家，必不以爲出母明矣。

translations.literal: If after Shi’s father died the mother soon perished in Shi’s house, clearly she would not have been treated as a divorced mother.
translations.idiomatic: Had she died in Wang Shi’s home right after his father, no one would call her “divorced.”

sentences.zh: 許諾之命一耳，以爲母于同居之時，至沒前子之門而不以爲母，此爲制離絕於二居，裁出否於意斷。

translations.literal: The promise was one and the same; while they lived together she was taken as mother, yet before the gate of the son from her earlier marriage she is not taken as mother—this is to legislate severance between two residences and to decide “divorced or not” by arbitrary whim.
translations.idiomatic: One promise cannot make her a mother in one house yet a stranger at her elder son’s gate—that invents a split household and lets whim rule “divorce.”

sentences.zh: 離絕之斷，非式而誰！

translations.literal: If the judgment of severance is not Shi’s, whose is it!
translations.idiomatic: If anyone broke the tie, it was Wang Shi himself!

sentences.zh: 假使二門之子皆此母之生，母戀前子，求去求絕，非禮於後家，還反又非禮於前門，去不可去，還不可還，則爲無寄之人也。

translations.literal: Suppose the sons of both households were all born of this same mother; the mother loves the earlier sons and seeks to leave and sever ties—this is unritual toward the later household, yet to return is again unritual toward the earlier gate; she cannot leave, cannot return, and becomes a person with nowhere to cling.
translations.idiomatic: Imagine sons in both houses by one mother who loves the first set and wants out—she wrongs the second family by leaving and the first by returning; trapped both ways, she belongs nowhere.

sentences.zh: 式必內盡匡諫，外極防閑，不絕明矣。

translations.literal: Shi surely ought inwardly to have remonstrated to the utmost and outwardly to have fenced her in strictly—clearly he should not have severed the bond.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Shi owed her fierce remonstrance and strict guard—never a rupture.

sentences.zh: 何至守不移於至親，略情禮於假繼乎！

translations.literal: How could he hold unyielding to distant kin yet stint feeling and ritual toward a nominal stepmother!
translations.idiomatic: How guard strangers’ feelings yet stint ritual toward the woman who raised him!

sentences.zh: 繼母如母，聖人之教。

translations.literal: “A stepmother is like a mother”—this is the teaching of the sages.
translations.idiomatic: The sages teach: a stepmother is a mother.

sentences.zh: 式爲國士，閨門之內犯禮違義，開闢未有，於父則無追亡之善，於母則無孝敬之道，存則去留自由，亡則合葬路人，可謂生事不以禮，死葬不以禮者也。

translations.literal: Shi is reckoned a leading knight of the state, yet within the inner quarters he violates ritual and duty, such as the age has not seen since creation; toward his father he shows no goodness in setting right what is past, toward his mother no way of filial respect; while alive she may go or stay at will, when dead she is buried with a stranger on the road—this may be called serving the living not by ritual and burying the dead not by ritual.
translations.idiomatic: A “stateworthy” who shames his inner chambers, fails his father’s memory, dishonors his mother, lets her wander alive and lie with strangers dead, breaks every rule of service to the living and dead.

sentences.zh: 虧損世教，不可以居人倫詮正之任。

translations.literal: He injures the moral instruction of the age and cannot occupy a post that rectifies human relationships.
translations.idiomatic: He corrupts public morals and cannot judge others’ conduct.

sentences.zh: 案侍中、司徒、臨潁公組敷宣五教，實在任人，而含容違禮，曾不貶黜；

translations.literal: Consider: Palace Attendant, Situ, Duke of Linying Zu spreads the five teachings and truly lies in appointing the right men, yet he tolerated violation of ritual and never demoted anyone;
translations.idiomatic: Zu Xian, Situ and duke of Linying, should spread the five bonds yet swallowed this breach without demotion;

sentences.zh: 揚州大中正、侍中、平望亭侯曄，[2]淮南大中正、散騎侍郎弘，顯執邦論，朝野取信，曾不能率禮正違，崇孝敬之教，並爲不勝其任。

translations.literal: Grand rectifier of Yangzhou, Palace Attendant, Village Marquis of Pingwang Ye[2], grand rectifier of Huainan, Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Hong, who openly wield state opinion and win the trust of court and countryside, were likewise unable to lead by ritual and correct the breach, to exalt the teaching of filial respect—they are all not equal to their charge.
translations.idiomatic: Ye [2], grand rectifier of Yangzhou, and Hong of Huainan, who shape national opinion, failed to enforce ritual or exalt filial duty—they too are unfit.

sentences.zh: 請以見事免組、曄、弘官，大鴻臚削爵土，廷尉結罪。

translations.literal: I ask that in accordance with the facts they be removed from office—Zu, Ye, and Hong—the Grand Keeper of the Seals be stripped of fief and rank, and the commandant of justice fix their guilt.”
translations.idiomatic: Dismiss Zu, Ye, and Hong, strip the grand herald of fief, and let the commandant of justice assign penalties.”

sentences.zh: 」疏奏，詔特原組等，式付鄉邑清議，廢棄終身。

translations.literal: ” When the memorial was presented, an edict specially pardoned Zu and the others, while Shi was handed to the village for pure discussion and cast aside for life.
translations.idiomatic: The throne pardoned the high ministers but handed Wang Shi to local “pure discussion” and barred him for life.

sentences.zh: 壼遷吏部尚書。

translations.literal: Kun was promoted to Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun became minister of personnel.

sentences.zh: 王含之難，加中軍將軍。

translations.literal: During the crisis of Wang Han, he was additionally named General of the Central Army.
translations.idiomatic: When Wang Han rebelled he was named general of the central army as well.

sentences.zh: 含滅，以功封建興縣公，尋遷領軍將軍。

translations.literal: When Han was destroyed, for merit he was enfeoffed as duke of Jianxing county and soon promoted to General Who Commands the Army.
translations.idiomatic: After Han fell he was made duke of Jianxing for merit, then general who commands the army.

sentences.zh: 明帝不豫，領尚書令，與王導等俱受顧命輔幼主。

translations.literal: When Emperor Ming was indisposed, he concurrently held Palace Secretary and, together with Wang Dao and others, received the testamentary charge to assist the young sovereign.
translations.idiomatic: As Emperor Ming sickened, Kun took palace secretary alongside Wang Dao and others in the regency for the boy emperor.

sentences.zh: 復拜右將軍，加給事中、尚書令。

translations.literal: He was again appointed General of the Right, with additional titles attendant-within-palace and palace secretary.
translations.idiomatic: He was named again General of the Right, plus attendant-within-palace and palace secretary.

sentences.zh: 帝崩，成帝即位，群臣進璽，司徒王導以疾不至。

translations.literal: When the emperor died and Emperor Cheng ascended, the ministers advanced the seal; Situ Wang Dao, citing illness, did not arrive.
translations.idiomatic: At Cheng’s accession the ministers brought the jade seal; Wang Dao, claiming illness, stayed away.

sentences.zh: 壼正色於朝曰：「王公豈社稷之臣邪！

translations.literal: Kun said with stern countenance at court, “Is Lord Wang not a minister of the altars of soil and grain!
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun snapped at court, “Is Minister Wang no longer a pillar of the state?

sentences.zh: 大行在殯，嗣皇未立，寧是人臣辭疾之時！

translations.literal: The late ruler lies in the coffined hall, the successor is not yet established—can this be the time for ministers to plead illness!”
translations.idiomatic: The late emperor lies in state, the heir is not yet enthroned—this is no hour for ministers to feign sickness!”

sentences.zh: 」導聞之，乃輿疾而至。

translations.literal: ” When Dao heard this, he then had himself carried in illness and came.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao heard, had himself carried in, and appeared.

sentences.zh: 皇太后臨朝，壼與庾亮對直省中，共參機要。

translations.literal: When the empress dowager held court, Kun together with Yu Liang kept straight watch in the palace secretariat and jointly participated in the crucial decisions of state.
translations.idiomatic: Under the empress dowager’s regency he and Yu Liang stood alternate duty in the secretariat and steered policy.

sentences.zh: 時召南陽樂謨爲郡中正，潁川庾怡爲廷尉評。

translations.literal: At that time Yue Mo of Nanyang was summoned as rectifier of the commandery, and Yu Yi of Yingchuan as reviewer for the commandant of justice.
translations.idiomatic: The court called Yue Mo of Nanyang as commandery rectifier and Yu Yi of Yingchuan as judicial reviewer.

sentences.zh: 謨、怡各稱父命不就。

translations.literal: Mo and Yi each cited a father’s command and would not take up office.
translations.idiomatic: Both men refused, pleading paternal orders.

sentences.zh: 壼奏曰：「人無非父而生，職無非事而立。

translations.literal: Kun memorialized, saying, “No man is born without a father, and no office is established without duties attached.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun wrote: “Every man has a father; every post carries duty.

sentences.zh: 有父必有命，居職必有悔。

translations.literal: Where there is a father there must be commands; where one holds office there must be regrets.
translations.idiomatic: Fathers give commands; offices bring second thoughts.

sentences.zh: 有家各私其子，此爲王者無人，職不軌物，官不立政。

translations.literal: If each family privately favors its own sons, then the king has no men, offices do not keep things within bounds, and government cannot establish policy.
translations.idiomatic: If every clan favors only its own, the king has no servants, posts lose their grip, and policy collapses.

sentences.zh: 如此則先聖之言廢，五教之訓塞，君臣之道散，上下之化替矣。

translations.literal: If it is so, then the words of the former sages are cast aside, the instructions of the five teachings are blocked, the way of ruler and minister is scattered, and the transformation of high and low is ruined.
translations.idiomatic: Then the sages’ teaching dies, the five bonds clog, ministerial duty frays, and order from top to bottom unravels.

sentences.zh: 樂廣以平夷稱，庾珉以忠篤顯，受寵聖世，身非己有，況及後嗣而可專哉！

translations.literal: Yue Guang was famed for leveling calm, Yu Min for loyal earnestness; they received favor in this sage age, and their persons were not their own to dispose of—how much less the offices of their posterity that they might monopolize them!
translations.idiomatic: Yue Guang and Yu Min were honored servants of the state, not masters of their own persons—much less may their sons treat public posts as heirlooms!

sentences.zh: 所居之職若順夫群心，則戰戍者之父母皆當以命子，不以處也。

translations.literal: If the posts they hold are to follow the crowd’s heart, then the parents of men on garrison duty should all use paternal commands to excuse their sons from taking up post.
translations.idiomatic: If whim rules, every soldier’s parents could forbid service.

sentences.zh: 若順謨父之意，則人皆不爲郡中正，人倫廢矣。

translations.literal: If one follows Mo’s father’s intent, then no one will serve as commandery rectifier, and human relationships will be cast away.
translations.idiomatic: Let Yue Mo’s father decide and no one will be a rectifier—society unravels.

sentences.zh: 順怡父之意，人皆不爲獄官，則刑辟息矣。

translations.literal: If one follows Yi’s father’s intent, then no one will be a prison officer, and punishments will cease.
translations.idiomatic: Let Yu Yi’s father decide and no one will judge cases—justice stops.

sentences.zh: 凡如是者，其可聽歟？

translations.literal: In all such cases, can it be permitted?
translations.idiomatic: Can we allow that?

sentences.zh: 若不可聽，何以許謨、怡之得稱父命乎！

translations.literal: If it cannot be permitted, on what ground may Mo and Yi be allowed to invoke a father’s command!
translations.idiomatic: If not, how can we let them hide behind “father’s orders”?

sentences.zh: 此爲謨以名父子可以虧法，怡是親戚可以自專。

translations.literal: This means that Mo, as a famous father’s son, may injure the law, and Yi, as a kinsman, may act on private whim.
translations.idiomatic: That would let a famous son break law and a kinsman rule himself.

sentences.zh: 以此二塗服人示世，臣所未悟也。

translations.literal: To convince the world by these two paths is something your servant has not understood.
translations.idiomatic: Those two precedents would teach the empire the wrong lesson.

sentences.zh: 宜一切班下，不得以私廢公。

translations.literal: It is fitting to issue a general order that none may discard the public for private ends.
translations.idiomatic: Issue a blanket rule: no private excuse may void public duty.

sentences.zh: 絕其表疏，以爲永制。

translations.literal: Cut off such memorial excuses and make it a standing statute.”
translations.idiomatic: Bar such petitions forever.”

sentences.zh: 」朝議以爲然。

translations.literal: ” Court discussion deemed it right.
translations.idiomatic: Court debate agreed.

sentences.zh: 謨、怡不得已，各居所職。

translations.literal: Mo and Yi, having no choice, each took up his office.
translations.idiomatic: Yue Mo and Yu Yi had to serve.

sentences.zh: 是時王導稱疾不朝，而私送車騎將軍郗鑒，壼奏以導虧法從私，無大臣之節。

translations.literal: At that time Wang Dao claimed illness and did not attend court, yet privately escorted General of Chariots and Cavalry Xi Jian; Kun memorialized that Dao violated the law to follow private feeling and lacked the integrity of a great minister.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao skipped court to bid Xi Jian farewell in private; Bian Kun impeached him for putting favor above law.

sentences.zh: 御史中丞鍾雅阿撓王典，不加準繩，並請免官。

translations.literal: Imperial Censor-in-chief Zhong Ya bent the royal statutes and did not apply correction; Kun asked that both be dismissed.
translations.idiomatic: Censor-in-chief Zhong Ya twisted the code and never censured him—Kun demanded both be cashiered.

sentences.zh: 雖事寢不行，舉朝震肅。

translations.literal: Although the matter in the end was not carried out, the whole court was awed and stern.
translations.idiomatic: The plea stalled, yet the whole bureaucracy trembled straight.

sentences.zh: 壼斷裁切直，不畏強禦，皆此類也。

translations.literal: Kun’s judgments were incisive and blunt; he did not fear the powerful—his conduct was all of this kind.
translations.idiomatic: His rulings were blunt and fearless—always thus.

sentences.zh: 壼榦實當官，以褒貶爲己任，勤於吏事，欲軌正督世，不肯苟同時好。

translations.literal: Kun was solid and practical in holding office, took praise and blame as his own charge, was diligent in clerical affairs, wished to set straight and oversee the age, and would not lightly agree with the fashions of the time.
translations.idiomatic: He ran office with iron diligence, lived for moral judgment, toiled over paperwork, meant to straighten the age, and spurned fashionable compromise.

sentences.zh: 然性不弘裕，才不副意，故爲諸名士所少，而無卓爾優譽。

translations.literal: Yet by nature he was not broad and tolerant, and his talent did not match his intent; therefore he was slighted by the various celebrated gentlemen and had no outstanding lofty reputation.
translations.idiomatic: He was narrow rather than magnanimous, and his gifts fell short of his zeal—so the great wits patronized him and he won no sparkling fame.

sentences.zh: 明帝深器之，於諸大臣而最任職。

translations.literal: Emperor Ming deeply esteemed him and, among the great ministers, entrusted him with the most substantive duties.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming valued him above the rest and piled real work on him.

sentences.zh: 阮孚每謂之曰：「卿恒無閑泰，常如含瓦石，不亦勞乎？

translations.literal: Ruan Fu often said to him, “You are never leisurely and at ease, but always as though holding tiles and stones in your mouth—is it not laborious?”
translations.idiomatic: Ruan Fu teased him: “You never rest easy, always as if chewing gravel—is that not exhausting?”

sentences.zh: 」壼曰：「諸君以道德恢弘，風流相尚，執鄙吝者，非壼而誰！

translations.literal: Kun said, “You gentlemen, with your vast virtue and ease, make fashion of one another; as for the one who holds to meanness and stinginess—if not Kun, who is it!”
translations.idiomatic: Kun answered: “You parade broad virtue and breezy grace; if someone must play the pinchpenny, it is I.”

sentences.zh: 」時貴游子弟多慕王澄、謝鯤爲達，壼厲色於朝曰：「悖禮傷教，罪莫斯甚！

translations.literal: ” At that time many noble youths admired Wang Cheng and Xie Kun for “transcendence”; Kun said with stern countenance at court, “To rebel against ritual and wound instruction—no crime is greater!
translations.idiomatic: When young lords aped Wang Cheng and Xie Kun’s “transcendence,” he thundered in court: “Nothing fouls the teaching of ritual more!

sentences.zh: 中朝傾覆，實由於此。

translations.literal: The overturning of the central court was truly caused by this.”
translations.idiomatic: That very fashion capsized the western capital.”

sentences.zh: 」欲奏推之。

translations.literal: ” He wished to memorialize and impeach them.
translations.idiomatic: He prepared impeachments.

sentences.zh: 王導、庾亮不從，乃止，然而聞者莫不折節。

translations.literal: Wang Dao and Yu Liang did not consent, so he stopped; yet among those who heard, none failed to restrain themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao and Yu Liang blocked him, yet everyone who heard checked himself.

sentences.zh: 時王導以勳德輔政，成帝每幸其宅，嘗拜導婦曹氏。

translations.literal: At that time Wang Dao, by merit and virtue, assisted the government; Emperor Cheng on each visit to his house once bowed to Dao’s wife, Lady Cao.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Cheng used to visit Wang Dao’s home and bow to Lady Cao, Wang’s wife.

sentences.zh: 侍中孔坦密表不宜拜。

translations.literal: Palace Attendant Kong Tan secretly memorialized that it was not fitting to bow.
translations.idiomatic: Kong Tan secretly said the emperor should not bow.

sentences.zh: [3]導聞之曰：「王茂弘駑痾耳，若卞望之之巖巖，刁玄亮之察察，戴若思之峰岠，當敢爾邪！

translations.literal: [3] When Dao heard it he said, “Wang Maohong is only a tired nag; if Bian Wangzhi stood as stern as a cliff, Diao Xuanliang as sharp as a knife’s edge, Dai Ruosi as towering as a peak—would they dare do this!”
translations.idiomatic: [3] Wang Dao sniffed: “I am a worn-out nag; had Bian Kun stood rock-hard, Diao Xie razor-keen, Dai Ruosi like a cliff—would anyone have dared?”

sentences.zh: 」壼廉潔儉素，居甚貧約。

translations.literal: Kun was incorrupt, frugal, and plain; his household was extremely poor and constrained.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun lived chaste, spare, and poor.

sentences.zh: 息當婚，詔特賜錢五十萬，固辭不受。

translations.literal: When his son was about to marry, an edict specially granted 500,000 cash, but he firmly declined and would not accept.
translations.idiomatic: For his son’s wedding the court sent fifty thousand strings; he refused outright.

sentences.zh: 後患面創，累乞解職。

translations.literal: Later, suffering from a facial sore, he repeatedly begged to be released from office.
translations.idiomatic: A facial ulcer later drove him to beg off his posts repeatedly.

sentences.zh: 拜光祿大夫，加散騎常侍。

translations.literal: He was appointed Palace Grandee and additionally Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
translations.idiomatic: He was named palace grandee with cavalier attendant-in-ordinary added.

sentences.zh: 時庾亮將徵蘇峻，言於朝曰：「峻狼子野心，終必爲亂。

translations.literal: At that time Yu Liang was about to summon Su Jun and said at court, “Jun has the heart of a wolf cub and in the end is sure to make rebellion.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Liang told court he would recall Su Jun: “Jun is wolf-hearted and will rebel.

sentences.zh: 今日徵之，縱不順命，爲禍猶淺。

translations.literal: If we summon him now, even should he disobey the command, the harm will still be shallow.
translations.idiomatic: Call him in now; even if he balks, the damage stays small.

sentences.zh: 若復經年，爲惡滋蔓，不可復制。

translations.literal: If we wait further years and let evil grow and spread, he can no longer be controlled.
translations.idiomatic: Let him grow a few more years and he cannot be stopped.

sentences.zh: 此是朝錯勸漢景帝早削七國事也。

translations.literal: This is the affair of Chao Cuo urging Emperor Jing of Han to pare the seven states early.”
translations.idiomatic: It is Chao Cuo urging Han Jingdi to clip the seven kingdoms early.”

sentences.zh: 」當時議者無以易之。

translations.literal: ” At that time none of the debaters could refute him.
translations.idiomatic: No one in debate could gainsay him.

sentences.zh: 壼固爭，謂亮曰：「峻擁強兵，多藏無賴，且逼近京邑，路不終朝，一旦有變，易爲蹉跌。

translations.literal: Kun firmly disputed and said to Liang, “Jun holds a strong host and shelters many knaves-errant, and moreover is close to the capital—less than a morning’s march; if suddenly there is a change, it is easy to stumble.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun fought him: “Jun commands strong troops and ruffians, sits a dawn march from the capital—any surprise could trip us.

sentences.zh: 宜深思遠慮，恐未可倉卒。

translations.literal: You ought to think deeply and plan far; I fear this cannot be done in haste.”
translations.idiomatic: Think long and hard—this cannot be rushed.”

sentences.zh: 」亮不納。

translations.literal: Liang did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Liang would not listen.

sentences.zh: 壼知必敗，與平南將軍溫嶠書曰：「元規召峻意定，懷此於邑。

translations.literal: Kun knew it was sure to fail; he wrote to General Who Pacifies the South, Wen Qiao, saying, “Yuankui’s mind to summon Jun is settled—my breast is full of sorrow over it.
translations.idiomatic: Knowing disaster loomed, he wrote Wen Qiao: “Yu Liang’s plan to recall Su Jun is fixed—I ache with worry.

sentences.zh: 溫生足下，柰此事何！

translations.literal: Master Wen, below you—what is to be done with this affair!”
translations.idiomatic: Wen Qiao, my friend—what can we do?

sentences.zh: 吾今所慮，是國之大事。

translations.literal: What I now worry over is the great affair of the state.
translations.idiomatic: This is the fate of the realm.

sentences.zh: 且峻已出狂意，而召之更速，必縱其群惡以向朝廷。

translations.literal: Moreover, Jun has already shown mad intent, and to summon him all the faster is sure to unleash his pack of evils toward the court.
translations.idiomatic: Jun already rages; hurrying the summons will loose his villains on the capital.

sentences.zh: 朝廷威力誠桓桓，交須接鋒履刃，尚不知便可即擒不？

translations.literal: The court’s awe-inspiring might is indeed majestic, yet we must cross blades and tread edges—do we even know whether he can be taken at once?
translations.idiomatic: Our army looks mighty, yet blade must meet blade—who says we seize him at a stroke?

sentences.zh: 王公亦同此情。

translations.literal: Lord Wang shares this feeling.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao feels the same dread.

sentences.zh: 吾與之爭甚懇切，不能如之何。

translations.literal: I argued with him most earnestly, yet could do nothing about it.
translations.idiomatic: I pleaded with him bitterly and could not move him.

sentences.zh: 本出足下爲外藩任，而今恨出足下在外。

translations.literal: Originally you were sent out to hold an outer screen; now I regret that you are outside.”
translations.idiomatic: We posted you on the frontier; now I rue that you are far away.”

sentences.zh: 若卿在內俱諫，必當相從。

translations.literal: If you had been within and had remonstrated together, he would surely have followed.
translations.idiomatic: Had you been in the capital to join the remonstrance, he might have yielded.

sentences.zh: 今內外戒嚴，四方有備，峻凶狂必無所至耳，恐不能使無傷，如何？

translations.literal: Now inner and outer are under strict guard and the four quarters are prepared; surely Jun’s fierce madness cannot reach here—yet I fear we cannot avoid harm altogether; what then?”
translations.idiomatic: Now defenses ring the city—Jun may not break in, yet bloodshed seems unavoidable—what then?”

sentences.zh: 」壼司馬任台勸壼宜畜良馬，以備不虞。

translations.literal: ” Kun’s army marshal Ren Tai urged Kun to keep good horses in reserve against the unexpected.
translations.idiomatic: His marshal Ren Tai begged him to stable good horses for flight.

sentences.zh: 壼笑曰：「以順逆論之，理無不濟。

translations.literal: Kun smiled and said, “Judging by compliance and rebellion, in principle there is nothing that will not succeed.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun smiled: “Right should conquer wrong—no need to doubt.

sentences.zh: 若萬一不然，豈須馬哉！

translations.literal: If by the myriad chance it is not so, would horses be needed!”
translations.idiomatic: If heaven betrays us, horses would not save us anyway!”

sentences.zh: 」峻果稱兵。

translations.literal: ” Jun indeed raised troops.
translations.idiomatic: Su Jun rose in arms.

sentences.zh: 壼復爲尚書令、右將軍、領右衛將軍，餘官如故。

translations.literal: Kun again became palace secretary, General of the Right, concurrently General of the Right Guard, his other posts as before.
translations.idiomatic: He resumed palace secretary, General of the Right, and right guard general.

sentences.zh: 峻至東陵口，詔以壼都督大桁東諸軍事、假節，復加領軍將軍、給事中。

translations.literal: When Jun reached Dongling Ford, an edict made Kun commander-in-chief of all military affairs east of the great floating bridge, with credential staff, and again added General Who Commands the Army and attendant-within-palace.
translations.idiomatic: When Jun reached Dongling Ford, orders made Bian Kun area commander east of the great pontoon, gave him the staff, and added command of the guards.

sentences.zh: 壼率郭默、趙胤等與峻大戰於西陵，爲峻所破。

translations.literal: Kun led Guo Mo, Zhao Yin, and others in a great battle with Jun at Xiling and was defeated by Jun.
translations.idiomatic: He led Guo Mo, Zhao Yin, and others against Su Jun at Xiling—and lost.

sentences.zh: 壼與鍾雅皆退還，死傷者以千數。

translations.literal: Kun and Zhong Ya both withdrew; the dead and wounded numbered in the thousands.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun and Zhong Ya fell back with thousands dead or wounded.

sentences.zh: 壼、雅並還節，詣闕謝罪。

translations.literal: Kun and Ya together returned their credential staffs and went to the palace gate to confess guilt.
translations.idiomatic: Both men returned their staffs and went to the gate to confess failure.

sentences.zh: 峻進攻青溪，壼與諸軍距擊，不能禁。

translations.literal: Jun advanced to attack Qingxi; Kun with the various armies resisted and struck but could not stop him.
translations.idiomatic: Su Jun drove on Qingxi; Bian Kun’s coalition could not hold him.

sentences.zh: 賊放火燒宮寺，六軍敗績。

translations.literal: The rebels set fire to the palaces and monasteries, and the six armies were routed.
translations.idiomatic: Rebel torches caught the palace compounds; the six armies collapsed.

sentences.zh: 壼時發背創，猶未合，力疾而戰，率厲散眾及左右吏數百人，攻賊麾下，苦戰，遂死之，時年四十八。

translations.literal: At that time Kun had a running sore on his back that had not yet closed, yet he fought in the grip of illness; he rallied scattered troops and several hundred clerks to his left and right, attacked the flank under Jun’s command banner, fought bitterly, and died in battle, aged forty-eight.
translations.idiomatic: Though a back ulcer still festered, he fought on, rallied hundreds of clerks and stragglers, struck Su Jun’s standard, and died in the melée at forty-eight.

sentences.zh: 二子眕、盱見父沒，相隨赴賊，同時見害。

translations.literal: His two sons, Zhen and Xu, seeing their father fall, followed each other into the rebel ranks and were killed together.
translations.idiomatic: His sons Zhen and Xu, seeing him fall, charged the rebels together and died beside him.

sentences.zh: 峻平，朝議贈壼左光祿大夫，加散騎常侍。

translations.literal: When Jun was crushed, court discussion posthumously awarded Kun Palace Grandee on the left, with addition of Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
translations.idiomatic: After Su Jun fell the court voted him posthumous palace grandee on the left plus cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.

sentences.zh: 尚書郎弘訥議以爲「死事之臣古今所重，卞令忠貞之節，當書于竹帛。

translations.literal: Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat Hong Ne argued that “ministers who die for their duty are esteemed in every age; the integrity of Director Bian should be written on bamboo and silk.
translations.idiomatic: Hong Ne urged: “Men who die for the state deserve lasting fame; Bian Kun’s steadfastness belongs on the record.”

sentences.zh: 今之追贈，實未副眾望，謂宜加鼎司之號，以旌忠烈之勳。

translations.literal: The present posthumous honors truly do not match popular expectation; I say the title of one of the three dukes should be added to signal his stalwart merit.”
translations.idiomatic: The current honors fall short; add a three-duke rank to mark his martyrdom.”

sentences.zh: 」司徒王導見議，進贈驃騎將軍，加侍中。

translations.literal: ” Situ Wang Dao, seeing the discussion, advanced the posthumous gift to General Who Inspires Might, with addition of palace attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao read the debate and raised the award to General Who Inspires Might with palace attendant.

sentences.zh: 訥重議曰：「夫事親莫大於孝，事君莫尚於忠。

translations.literal: Ne argued again, saying, “In serving kin nothing is greater than filial piety; in serving the ruler nothing is higher than loyalty.
translations.idiomatic: Hong Ne pressed again: “Filial piety tops family duty; loyalty tops service to the throne.

sentences.zh: 唯孝也，故能盡敬竭誠；

translations.literal: Only with filial piety can one exhaust reverence and pour out sincerity;
translations.idiomatic: Filial devotion yields full reverence;

sentences.zh: 唯忠也，故能見危授命。

translations.literal: only with loyalty can one, seeing peril, hand over one’s life.
translations.idiomatic: loyalty alone makes men die when danger calls.

sentences.zh: 此在三之大節，臣子之極行也。

translations.literal: These are the great nodes of the three relationships, the utmost conduct of ministers and sons.
translations.idiomatic: These are the pillars of the three bonds, the crown of minister and son alike.

sentences.zh: 案壼委質三朝，盡規翼亮，遭世險難，存亡以之。

translations.literal: Consider: Kun pledged himself to three courts, exhaustively remonstrating and aiding the radiance; he met a perilous age and pledged life or death to it.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Kun served three reigns with full remonstrance; he staked life and fortune on a dark time.

sentences.zh: 受顧託之重，居端右之任，擁衛至尊，則有保傅之恩；

translations.literal: He received the heavy charge of testamentary trust, occupied the chief post at the right, and in guarding the august supreme had the kindness of a guardian and tutor;
translations.idiomatic: He bore the regent’s charge at the summit of state and shielded the emperor like a tutor;

sentences.zh: 正色在朝，則有匪躬之節。

translations.literal: with stern countenance at court he had the integrity of one who does not spare himself.
translations.idiomatic: in court he showed the stern selflessness of a true minister.

sentences.zh: 賊峻造逆，戮力致討，身當矢旝，再對賊鋒，父子并命，可謂破家爲國，守死勤事。

translations.literal: When the rebel Jun created treason, he exhausted his strength to campaign against him, personally braving arrows and banner, twice facing the rebels’ edge; father and sons together gave their lives—this may be called ruining one’s household for the state and dying in diligent service.
translations.idiomatic: Against Su Jun he threw his whole house into the fight, took arrows at the van twice, and fell with both sons—utter ruin for the throne’s sake.

sentences.zh: 昔許男疾終，猶蒙二等之贈，況壼伏節國難者乎！

translations.literal: In old days, when the lord of Xu died of illness, he still received a gift of the second rank; how much more Kun, who laid down his life for the state’s peril!”
translations.idiomatic: Even Xu’s lord won second-rank honors on a sickbed—how much more Bian Kun who died for the realm!”

sentences.zh: 夫賞疑從重，況在不疑！

translations.literal: In doubtful rewards one favors generosity; how much more where there is no doubt!
translations.idiomatic: When merit is plain, reward should be generous—here doubt does not exist!

sentences.zh: 謂可上準許穆，下同嵇紹，則允合典謨，克厭眾望。

translations.literal: I say one may take the high mark of Xu Mu and the lower of Ji Shao, and then it will accord with the canons and satisfy all hopes.”
translations.idiomatic: Match the high precedent of Xu Mu and the lower of Ji Shao—then rites and public hope align.”

sentences.zh: 」於是改贈壼侍中、驃騎將軍、開府儀同三司，諡曰忠貞，祠以太牢。

translations.literal: ” Thereupon the posthumous honors were changed to palace attendant, General Who Inspires Might, opening of a princely mansion with three-offices parity, posthumous name “Loyal and True,” and sacrifice with the grand victim.
translations.idiomatic: The court reissued patent: palace attendant, General Who Inspires Might, three-offices mansion, styled “Loyal and True,” with the great sacrifice.

sentences.zh: 贈世子眕散騎侍郎，眕弟盱奉車都尉。

translations.literal: The heir apparent’s son Zhen was posthumously given Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Zhen’s younger brother Xu was given Colonel Who Conveys the Carriage.
translations.idiomatic: His son Zhen received posthumous gentleman cavalier; the younger Xu became carriage colonel.

sentences.zh: 眕母裴氏撫二子尸哭曰：「父爲忠臣，汝爲孝子，夫何恨乎！

translations.literal: Lady Pei, Zhen’s mother, stroked the corpses of her two sons and wept, saying, “Your father was a loyal minister; you are filial sons—what regret can there be!”
translations.idiomatic: Lady Pei clasped her dead sons: “Your father died loyal; you died filial—what room for grief?”

sentences.zh: 」徵士翟湯聞之歎曰：「父死於君，子死於父，忠孝之道，萃于一門。

translations.literal: ” Recluse Zhai Tang, hearing it, sighed and said, “The father died for the lord, the sons died for the father—the way of loyalty and filial piety is gathered in one gate.”
translations.idiomatic: Recluse Zhai Tang sighed: “Father for sovereign, sons for father—loyalty and filial piety met in one door.”

sentences.zh: 」眕子誕嗣。

translations.literal: ” Zhen’s son Dan succeeded.
translations.idiomatic: Dan, Zhen’s son, inherited the line.

sentences.zh: 咸康六年，成帝追思壼，下詔曰：「壼立朝忠恪，喪身兇寇，所封懸遠，租秩薄少，妻息不贍，以爲慨然！

translations.literal: In the sixth year of Xiankang, Emperor Cheng, recalling Kun with feeling, issued an edict saying, “Kun stood in court loyal and reverent and lost his body to fierce bandits; the enfeoffment hangs far away, rents and stipends are thin and few, and his wife and children are not provided for—this fills us with sorrow!
translations.idiomatic: In 340 Emperor Cheng remembered Bian Kun: “He served with utter loyalty and fell to rebels; his fief lies far, income thin, and his widow and children lack support—we grieve!

sentences.zh: 可給實口廩。

translations.literal: Let real mouths be supplied from the granaries.”
translations.idiomatic: Grant his household state grain by the mouth.”

sentences.zh: 」其後盜發壼墓，尸僵，鬢髮蒼白，面如生，兩手悉拳，爪甲穿達手背。

translations.literal: ” Later robbers opened Kun’s tomb; the corpse was stiff, the temples white as ash, the face as if alive, and both hands were clenched so that the nails pierced through the backs of the hands.
translations.idiomatic: Later tomb raiders broke in: his body lay rigid, hair white, face lifelike, fists clenched until nails pierced the backs of his hands.

sentences.zh: 安帝詔給錢十萬，以修塋兆。

translations.literal: Emperor An’s edict granted 100,000 cash to repair the tomb precinct.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor An allotted a hundred thousand cash to restore the grave.

sentences.zh: 壼第三子瞻，位至廣州刺史。

translations.literal: Kun’s third son Zhan rose to Inspector of Guang Province.
translations.idiomatic: His third son Bian Zhan became inspector of Guang.

sentences.zh: 瞻弟眈，尚書郎。

translations.literal: Zhan’s younger brother Dan was a gentleman of the Palace Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Zhan’s brother Dan served as palace gentleman.

sentences.zh: 從父兄敦

translations.literal: Paternal cousin Dun.
translations.idiomatic: His paternal cousin Bian Dun.

sentences.zh: 敦字仲仁。

translations.literal: Dun, courtesy name Zhongren.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Dun, style Zhongren.

sentences.zh: 父俊，清真有檢識，以名理著稱。

translations.literal: His father Jun was pure and true, with restraint and insight, and was famed for clear principles.
translations.idiomatic: His father Bian Jun was upright, discriminating, and celebrated for principled debate.

sentences.zh: 其鄉人郤詵恃才陵傲俊兄弟，俊等亦以門盛輕詵，相視如讎。

translations.literal: His fellow townsman Xi Shen relied on talent to bully and slight Jun and his brothers; Jun and the others, because their gate was eminent, in turn despised Shen, and they eyed each other like enemies.
translations.idiomatic: Xi Shen bullied the Bian brothers with his talent; they despised him in turn for his lesser house, and the two camps glared like foes.

sentences.zh: 詵以楊駿故吏被繫，俊時爲尚書郎，案其獄，詵懼不免，俊平心斷決正之，詵卒以免，而猶不悛。

translations.literal: Shen, as a former clerk of Yang Jun, was bound in fetters; at the time Jun was a gentleman of the Palace Secretariat and handled his case; Shen feared he would not escape, but Jun with even mind judged and set him aright, and Shen in the end was spared, yet still did not reform.
translations.idiomatic: Xi Shen, Yang Jun’s old clerk, was jailed; Bian Jun as palace gentleman tried the case fairly and freed him, yet Xi Shen never mended his ways.

sentences.zh: 後爲左丞，復奏陷卞氏。

translations.literal: Later, as left aide, he again memorialized to ruin the Bian clan.
translations.idiomatic: Later as left aide he tried again to destroy the Bians by memorial.

sentences.zh: 俊歷位汝南相、廷尉卿。

translations.literal: Jun rose through posts to chancellor of Runan and commandant of justice.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Jun became Runan chancellor and commandant of justice.

sentences.zh: 敦弱冠仕州郡，辟司空府，稍遷太子舍人、尚書郎，朝士多稱之。

translations.literal: At the capping age Dun served in province and commandery, was summoned to the directorate of works, and by stages rose to Gentleman Attendant of the heir apparent and gentleman of the Palace Secretariat; court gentlemen much praised him.
translations.idiomatic: After his capping he served locally, entered the works directorate, rose to heir’s attendant and palace gentleman, and won wide praise at court.

sentences.zh: 東海王越聞，召以爲主簿。

translations.literal: Prince Sima Yue of the East Sea heard of him and summoned him as chief clerk.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Yue of the East Sea made him chief clerk.

sentences.zh: 王彌逼洛，敦及胡毋輔之勸越擊王彌，而王衍、潘滔共執不聽，敦庭爭苦至，眾咸壯之。

translations.literal: When Wang Mi pressed Luoyang, Dun together with Hu Wuzhi urged Yue to strike Wang Mi, but Wang Yan and Pan Tao together seized control and would not listen; Dun argued bitterly in court to the utmost, and the crowd all thought him heroic.
translations.idiomatic: As Wang Mi threatened Luoyang, Dun and Hu Wuzhi begged Sima Yue to attack; Wang Yan and Pan Tao blocked the plan while Dun shouted himself hoarse in open court—the crowd admired his nerve.

sentences.zh: 出補汝南內史。

translations.literal: He went out to fill the vacancy as interior minister of Runan.
translations.idiomatic: He went out as interior minister of Runan.

sentences.zh: 元帝之爲鎮東，請爲軍諮祭酒，不就。

translations.literal: When Emperor Yuan was east-general, he asked Dun to be libationer-adviser of the army, but Dun did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan as east-general wanted him as army libationer; he declined.

sentences.zh: 征南將軍山簡以爲司馬。

translations.literal: General Who Conquers the South, Shan Jian, made him marshal.
translations.idiomatic: Shan Jian named him marshal.

sentences.zh: 尋而王如、杜曾相繼爲亂，簡乃使敦監沔北七郡軍事、振威將軍、領江夏相，戍夏口。

translations.literal: Soon Wang Ru and Du Zeng rose in succession; Jian then had Dun supervise military affairs in seven commanderies north of the Mian, as General Who Rouses Might, concurrently grand administrator of Jiangxia, garrisoned at Xiakou.
translations.idiomatic: When Wang Ru and Du Zeng revolted, Shan Jian put him over seven northern Han commanderies as General Who Rouses Might and Jiangxia administrator, based at Xiakou.

sentences.zh: 敦攻討沔中皆平。

translations.literal: Dun attacked and campaigned until all the middle Han was pacified.
translations.idiomatic: He cleared the Han basin by force.

sentences.zh: 既而杜弢寇湘中，加敦征討大都督。

translations.literal: Afterward Du Tao raided Xiang commanderies, and Dun was additionally named supreme area commander for conquest.
translations.idiomatic: When Du Tao struck Xiang, he became grand commander of suppression.

sentences.zh: 伐弢有功，賜爵安陵亭侯。

translations.literal: For merit in campaigning against Tao he was enfeoffed as village marquis of Anling.
translations.idiomatic: Crushing Du Tao won him the village marquisate of Anling.

sentences.zh: 鎮東大將軍王敦請爲軍司。

translations.literal: General Who Guards the East, Wang Dun, asked him to be army director.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun, east-guarding general, recruited him as army director.

sentences.zh: 中興建，拜太子左衛率。

translations.literal: When the Restoration was founded, he was appointed colonel of the left guard of the heir apparent.
translations.idiomatic: At Eastern Jin’s founding he became colonel of the heir’s left guard.

sentences.zh: 時石勒侵逼淮泗，帝備求良將可以式遏邊境者，公卿舉敦，除征虜將軍、徐州刺史，鎮泗口。

translations.literal: At that time Shi Le pressed against the Huai and Si region; the emperor prepared to seek good generals who could check the border, and the dukes and ministers raised Dun; he was appointed General Who Conquers Captives, Inspector of Xu Province, and stationed at Sikou.
translations.idiomatic: As Shi Le threatened Huai and Si, the court picked Bian Dun for General Who Conquers Captives and Xu inspector at Sikou.

sentences.zh: 及勒寇彭城，敦自度力不能支，與征北將軍王邃退保盱眙，賊勢遂張，淮北諸郡多爲所陷，竟以畏懦貶秩三等，爲鷹揚將軍。

translations.literal: When Le raided Pengcheng, Dun reckoned his strength could not sustain the defense and, together with General Who Conquers the North, Wang Sui, withdrew to defend Xuyi; the bandit power then swelled, and most commanderies north of the Huai fell to them; in the end, for cowardice he was demoted three ranks and made General Who Displays Might.
translations.idiomatic: He judged he could not hold Pengcheng, retreated with Wang Sui to Xuyi, lost the Huai north, and was stripped three ranks for cowardice to General Who Displays Might.

sentences.zh: 徵拜大司農。

translations.literal: He was summoned and appointed Minister of Agriculture.
translations.idiomatic: He was recalled as minister of agriculture.

sentences.zh: 王敦表爲征虜將軍、都督石頭軍事。

translations.literal: Wang Dun memorialized him as General Who Conquers Captives and commander of Stone Citadel forces.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun nominated him to command Stone Citadel as General Who Conquers Captives.

sentences.zh: 明帝之討王敦也，以爲鎮南將軍、假節。

translations.literal: When Emperor Ming campaigned against Wang Dun, Dun was named General Who Guards the South with credential staff.
translations.idiomatic: During Emperor Ming’s war on Wang Dun he received the southern guard generalcy with staff.

sentences.zh: 事平，更拜尚書，以功封益陽侯。

translations.literal: When the affair was settled, he was again appointed palace secretary and, for merit, enfeoffed as marquis of Yiyang.
translations.idiomatic: After peace he became palace secretary and marquis of Yiyang for merit.

sentences.zh: 徙光祿勳，出爲都督安南將軍、湘州刺史、假節。

translations.literal: He was shifted to Minister of the Imperial Clan and sent out as area commander, General Who Pacifies the South, Inspector of Xiang Province, with credential staff.
translations.idiomatic: He moved to minister of the imperial clan, then area commander as General Who Pacifies the South and Xiang inspector with staff.

sentences.zh: 尋進征南將軍，固辭不拜。

translations.literal: Soon he was advanced to General Who Conquers the South but firmly declined and would not accept.
translations.idiomatic: A promotion to south-conquering general followed; he refused it flatly.

sentences.zh: 蘇峻反，溫嶠、庾亮移檄征鎮同赴京師。

translations.literal: When Su Jun rebelled, Wen Qiao and Yu Liang circulated proclamations summoning garrisons to march on the capital together.
translations.idiomatic: Su Jun’s revolt brought joint summons from Wen Qiao and Yu Liang to every garrison.

sentences.zh: 敦擁兵不下，又不給軍糧，唯遣督護荀璲領數百人隨大軍而已。

translations.literal: Dun held his troops back from descending, supplied no army grain, and only sent supervisor Xun Sui with several hundred men to follow the great host—that was all.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Dun kept his army idle, sent no grain, and detached a few hundred men under Xun Sui to trail the main force.

sentences.zh: 時朝野莫不怪歎，獨陶侃亦切齒忿之。

translations.literal: At that time none in court or countryside did not marvel and sigh; only Tao Kan likewise gnashed his teeth in rage at him.
translations.idiomatic: Court and country gasped; Tao Kan alone ground his teeth in fury.

sentences.zh: [4]峻平，侃奏敦阻軍顧望，不赴國難，無大臣之節，請檻車收付廷尉。

translations.literal: [4] When Jun was crushed, Kan memorialized that Dun had blocked the army, looked two ways, and failed to answer the state’s peril, lacking the integrity of a great minister; he asked that Dun be taken in a caged cart and delivered to the commandant of justice.
translations.idiomatic: [4] After Su Jun fell, Tao Kan impeached Bian Dun for holding back his host, watching from the fence, and shirking the crisis—unworthy of a great minister—and demanded the caged cart.

sentences.zh: 丞相王導以喪亂之後宜加寬宥，轉安南將軍、廣州刺史。

translations.literal: Chancellor Wang Dao, because after the disasters and turmoil leniency was fitting, transferred him to General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Guang Province.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao, favoring mercy after the chaos, banished him to Guang as General Who Pacifies the South instead.

sentences.zh: 病不之職。

translations.literal: Illness kept him from taking up the post.
translations.idiomatic: Sickness stopped him from going south.

sentences.zh: 徵爲光祿大夫，領少府。

translations.literal: He was summoned as palace grandee, concurrently junior minister of the palace.
translations.idiomatic: He was recalled palace grandee with junior palace minister added.

sentences.zh: 敦既不討蘇峻，常懷愧恥，名論自此虧矣。

translations.literal: Dun, because he had not campaigned against Su Jun, always harbored shame and disgrace, and his reputation from this point was diminished.
translations.idiomatic: For sitting out Su Jun’s revolt he lived in shame and his name never recovered.

sentences.zh: 尋以憂卒，追贈本官，加散騎常侍，諡曰敬。

translations.literal: Soon he died of grief; posthumously he was awarded his former office, with addition of Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, posthumous name “Reverent.”
translations.idiomatic: He died soon after, broken; the court restored his titles, added cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, and styled him “Reverent.”

sentences.zh: 子滔嗣。

translations.literal: His son Tao succeeded.
translations.idiomatic: His heir Bian Tao carried the line.

sentences.zh: 劉超字世瑜，琅邪臨沂人，漢城陽景王章之後也。

translations.literal: Liu Chao, courtesy name Shiyu, was a native of Linyi in Langya and a descendant of Prince Jing of Chengyang, Zhang of Han.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Chao, style Shiyu, came from Linyi in Langya and traced descent from Liu Zhang, the Han Prince Jing of Chengyang.

sentences.zh: 章七世孫封臨沂縣慈鄉侯，子孫因家焉。

translations.literal: In the seventh generation of Zhang’s line a descendant was enfeoffed marquis of Cixiang in Linyi county, and his sons and grandsons therefore made their home there.
translations.idiomatic: Seven generations on, a branch received the Cixiang marquisate in Linyi and settled there.

sentences.zh: 父和，爲琅邪國上軍將軍。

translations.literal: His father He was senior general of the army in the princedom of Langya.
translations.idiomatic: His father Liu He commanded the princely army of Langya.

sentences.zh: 超少有志尚，爲縣小吏，稍遷琅邪國記室掾。

translations.literal: Chao in youth had high aims; he was a petty clerk of the county and by stages rose to recorder-clerk of the princedom of Langya.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Chao rose from county clerk to Langya’s recorder.

sentences.zh: 以忠謹清慎爲元帝所拔，恒親侍左右，遂從渡江，轉安東府舍人，專掌文檄。

translations.literal: For loyalty, carefulness, clarity, and prudence he was singled out by Emperor Yuan, constantly attending close at hand; he therefore followed in crossing the Yangzi, was transferred to Gentleman Attendant of the east-peace general’s headquarters, and exclusively managed documents and proclamations.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan prized his loyalty and caution, kept him at his side across the river, made him attendant at the east-peace headquarters, and put all papers in his hands.

sentences.zh: 相府建，又爲舍人。

translations.literal: When the chancellor’s headquarters was established, he again became attendant.
translations.idiomatic: When the chancellor’s office opened he stayed on as attendant.

sentences.zh: 于時天下擾亂，伐叛討貳，超自以職在近密，而書跡與帝手筆相類，乃絕不與人交書。

translations.literal: At that time the realm was in turmoil with campaigns against rebels and traitors; Chao, because his duty lay close and secret and his handwriting resembled the emperor’s own brush, therefore utterly refused to exchange letters with others.
translations.idiomatic: With the empire at war and his hand like the emperor’s script, he refused all private correspondence.

sentences.zh: 時出休沐，閉門不通賓客，由是漸得親密。

translations.literal: When he went out on rest-leave, he closed his gate and would not receive guests; by this means he gradually won still greater intimacy.
translations.idiomatic: On leave he barred his gate to visitors and so grew still closer to the throne.

sentences.zh: 以左右勤勞，賜爵原鄉亭侯，食邑七百戶，轉行參軍。

translations.literal: For diligence at the sovereign’s side he was enfeoffed as village marquis of Yuanxiang with a fief of seven hundred households and transferred to acting staff adviser.
translations.idiomatic: For tireless service he received the Yuanxiang village marquisate, seven hundred households, and acting staff adviser.

sentences.zh: 中興建，爲中書舍人，拜騎都尉、奉朝請。

translations.literal: When the Restoration was founded, he became gentleman of the secretariat, was appointed captain of cavalry and gentleman for court audience.
translations.idiomatic: At the Restoration he entered the secretariat as gentleman, cavalry captain, and gentleman at court.

sentences.zh: 時臺閣初建，庶績未康，超職典文翰，而畏慎靜密，彌見親待。

translations.literal: At that time the ministries were first set up and the myriad tasks were not yet at peace; Chao, though his office governed brush and ink, through fear and careful quiet secrecy was all the more treated with intimacy.
translations.idiomatic: As ministries took shape his writing office stayed discreet and won deeper trust.

sentences.zh: 加以處身清苦，衣不重帛，家無儋石之儲。

translations.literal: Added to this, he kept his person pure and hard; he did not layer silks on his clothes, and his house had not a dan or shi of stored grain.
translations.idiomatic: He lived sparely—no doubled silks, no granary stores.

sentences.zh: 每帝所賜，皆固辭曰：「凡陋小臣，橫竊賞賜，無德而祿，殃咎足懼。

translations.literal: Whenever the emperor bestowed gifts, he firmly declined, saying, “A mean and petty minister who steals rewards across his station, enjoying stipend without virtue—disaster and blame are things to be feared.”
translations.idiomatic: Imperial gifts he refused: “A petty clerk who steals reward without merit courts calamity.”

sentences.zh: 」帝嘉之，不奪其志。

translations.literal: ” The emperor praised him and did not wrest away his resolve.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor praised him and let him decline.

sentences.zh: 尋出補句容令，推誠於物，爲百姓所懷。

translations.literal: Soon he went out to fill the vacancy as magistrate of Jurong; he pushed sincerity upon things and was cherished by the common people.
translations.idiomatic: As magistrate of Jurong he dealt honestly with people and won their hearts.

sentences.zh: 常年賦稅，主者常自四出結評百姓家貲。

translations.literal: In ordinary years for taxes and levies the chief clerks always went out in four directions to knot and assess the property of the common households.
translations.idiomatic: Yearly tax clerks used to fan out to inventory every household’s goods.

sentences.zh: 至超，但作大函，邨別付之，使各自書家產，投函中訖，送還縣。

translations.literal: When it came to Chao, he only made a large box, gave one to each village separately, and had them each write their own household property, cast it into the box when finished, and send it back to the county.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Chao instead dropped a sealed chest in each hamlet and let families declare their own holdings.

sentences.zh: 百姓依實投上，課輸所入，有踰常年。

translations.literal: The common people according to the truth cast them in, and the levies entered exceeded those of ordinary years.
translations.idiomatic: Honest returns poured in, and revenue beat ordinary years.

sentences.zh: 入爲中書通事郎。

translations.literal: He entered as gentleman for general secretariat business.
translations.idiomatic: He returned to the secretariat as general-affairs gentleman.

sentences.zh: 以父憂去官。

translations.literal: He left office for mourning for his father.
translations.idiomatic: Father’s death took him home for mourning.

sentences.zh: 既葬，屬王敦稱兵，詔超復職，又領安東上將軍。

translations.literal: After the burial, it happened that Wang Dun raised troops; an edict recalled Chao to office and also put him in charge of the heir’s east-supreme general.
translations.idiomatic: Before mourning ended Wang Dun rebelled; an edict recalled him and attached him to the heir’s eastern supreme army.

sentences.zh: 尋六軍敗散，唯超案兵直衛，帝感之，遣歸終喪禮。

translations.literal: Soon the six armies were scattered in defeat; only Chao held his troops in straight guard of the emperor; the emperor was moved and sent him back to complete the mourning rites.
translations.idiomatic: When the six armies broke, only Liu Chao held the palace guard; the moved emperor sent him back to finish mourning.

sentences.zh: 及錢鳳構禍，超招合義士，從明帝征鳳。

translations.literal: When Qian Feng brewed disaster, Chao gathered righteous knights and followed Emperor Ming to campaign against Feng.
translations.idiomatic: When Qian Feng struck, he rallied loyalists for Emperor Ming’s campaign.

sentences.zh: 事平，以功封零陵伯。

translations.literal: When the affair was settled, for merit he was enfeoffed as earl of Lingling.
translations.idiomatic: Peace won him the earldom of Lingling.

sentences.zh: 超家貧，妻子不贍，帝手詔褒之，賜以魚米，超辭不受。

translations.literal: Chao’s household was poor; his wife and children were not provided for; the emperor by his own hand issued an edict praising him and granted fish and rice, but Chao declined and would not accept.
translations.idiomatic: His family starved though he was now an earl; the emperor sent fish and rice by personal edict, yet he refused.

sentences.zh: 超後須純色牛，市不可得，啟買官外廄牛，詔便以賜之。

translations.literal: Later Chao needed a cow of uniform color; none could be bought in the market; he petitioned to buy a cow from the official outer stable, and an edict thereupon bestowed one on him.
translations.idiomatic: When he needed a solid-colored ox and the market had none, the throne gave him one from the imperial herd.

sentences.zh: 出爲義興太守。

translations.literal: He went out as grand administrator of Yixing.
translations.idiomatic: He governed Yixing as grand administrator.

sentences.zh: 未幾，徵拜中書侍郎。

translations.literal: Before long he was summoned and appointed gentleman of the secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as secretariat gentleman.

sentences.zh: 拜受往還，朝廷莫有知者。

translations.literal: He went to receive appointment and return without anyone in the court knowing.
translations.idiomatic: He took the post in such secrecy that the court never noticed the round trip.

sentences.zh: 會帝崩，穆后臨朝，遷射聲校尉。

translations.literal: It happened that the emperor died; when Empress Mu held court, he was promoted to colonel of the sound-shooting guard.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor died; under Empress Dowager Mu he became colonel of the sound-shooting guard.

sentences.zh: 時軍校無兵，義興人多義隨超，因統其眾以宿衛，號爲「君子營」。

translations.literal: At that time the military school had no troops; many men of Yixing, out of righteousness, followed Chao, so he commanded their host for palace watch and it was styled the “gentlemen’s camp.”
translations.idiomatic: That corps had no soldiers, so Yixing volunteers who loved him formed the “gentlemen’s camp” for palace duty.

sentences.zh: 咸和初，遭母憂去官，衰服不離身，朝夕號泣，朔望輒步至墓所，哀感路人。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Xianhe, he met mourning for his mother and left office; mourning garments did not leave his body, morning and evening he wailed; at each new and full moon he always walked to the grave site, his grief moving passersby on the road.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Xianhe he mourned his mother to resignation, never doffed sackcloth, wept day and night, and walked each month to her grave until travelers wept with him.

sentences.zh: 及蘇峻謀逆，超代趙胤爲左衛將軍。

translations.literal: When Su Jun plotted rebellion, Chao replaced Zhao Yin as General of the Left Guard.
translations.idiomatic: When Su Jun rebelled, Liu Chao succeeded Zhao Yin as general of the left guard.

sentences.zh: 時京邑大亂，朝士多遣家人入東避難。

translations.literal: At that time the capital was in great turmoil, and many court gentlemen sent their families east to escape disaster.
translations.idiomatic: As the capital collapsed, courtiers shipped kin eastward for safety.

sentences.zh: 義興故吏欲迎超家，而超不聽，盡以妻孥入處宮內。

translations.literal: Former clerks of Yixing wished to welcome Chao’s household, but Chao would not listen and moved his wife and children entirely into the palace precincts.
translations.idiomatic: Yixing old staff offered to shelter his family; he refused and moved wife and children inside the palace walls.

sentences.zh: 及王師敗績，王導以超爲右衛將軍，親侍成帝。

translations.literal: When the royal army was routed, Wang Dao made Chao General of the Right Guard to attend personally on Emperor Cheng.
translations.idiomatic: After the imperial rout Wang Dao named him right guard to stay at the boy emperor’s side.

sentences.zh: 屬太后崩，軍衛禮章損闕，超躬率將士奉營山陵。

translations.literal: It happened that the empress dowager died; military guard and ritual regulations were damaged and lacking; Chao personally led generals and soldiers to tend the mausoleum hills.
translations.idiomatic: When the empress dowager died and rites frayed, he led the guard to tend her tomb himself.

sentences.zh: 峻遷車駕石頭，時天大雨，道路沈陷，超與侍中鍾雅步侍左右，賊給馬不肯騎，而悲哀慷慨。

translations.literal: Jun moved the imperial carriage to Stone Citadel; at that time heaven sent great rain and the roads sank and mired; Chao together with Palace Attendant Zhong Ya walked in attendance to the left and right; the rebels offered horses but they would not ride, and they were mournful and stirred with passion.
translations.idiomatic: Su Jun dragged the court to Stone Citadel through pouring rain and ruined roads; Liu Chao and Zhong Ya walked beside the boy emperor, refused rebel horses, and wept with rage.

sentences.zh: 峻聞之，甚不平，然未敢加害，而以其所親信許方等補司馬督、殿中監，外託宿衛，內實防禦超等。

translations.literal: When Jun heard of it, he was greatly resentful, yet did not dare to harm them outright; instead he filled the posts of army marshal supervisor and palace-inside supervisor with his trusted men such as Xu Fang, ostensibly for night watch but in truth to guard against Chao and the others inwardly.
translations.idiomatic: Su Jun fumed yet dared not strike; he packed the palace guard with men like Xu Fang—nominally on watch, really watching Liu Chao.

sentences.zh: 時饑饉米貴，峻等問遺，一無所受，繾綣朝夕，臣節愈恭。

translations.literal: At that time famine made rice dear; when Jun and his men made inquiries and sent gifts, they accepted nothing at all; day and night they clung close, and their integrity as ministers grew ever more reverent.
translations.idiomatic: Famine made rice gold; Su Jun’s bribes they refused, clinging to the emperor night and day with tighter loyalty.

sentences.zh: 帝時年八歲，雖幽厄之中，超猶啟授孝經、論語。

translations.literal: The emperor at the time was eight sui; though in peril and constraint, Chao still opened instruction and taught him the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor was only eight, yet Liu Chao taught him the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects even in captivity.

sentences.zh: 溫嶠等至，峻猜忌朝士，而超爲帝所親遇，疑之尤甚。
